scenario: Live two-tab WebRTC room, real WebGPU on both devices, strategy 'even' (forced 14+14 split). Host sends a chat prompt; while generation is in flight, the host's own 'Drop a device' instrument (room.dropWorker(), the same path a real disconnect takes) removes the sole worker. Matches IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md Phase A, Step A.4, Option 1 (down to one survivor -> falls back to solo) -- the direct GPU analog of tests/recovery.test.mjs's CPU case.

codeChangesUnderTest.change: this.engine?.dispose?.() added at the top of _load() and before the model-changed branch's this.engine = null in the 'deal' handler, so a superseded GpuEngineAdapter's WebGPU device is destroyed instead of leaked.
codeChangesUnderTest.priorState: grep dispose room/room.js matched nothing -- confirmed by inspection before this session's edits.

codeChangesUnderTest.change: Exported checkDeviceLost(device); GpuEngineAdapter.embedRun/runHidden/headFromHidden now catch, call it, and rethrow -- so a device lost mid-generation (not just mid-load) surfaces the same honest 'GPU device lost (...)' message load-time loss already got, instead of a raw Dawn exception.
codeChangesUnderTest.liveTrigger: Not exercised live this session -- no actual WebGPU device-lost event occurred (the failure mode tested here is peer disconnect, not GPU driver/device loss). Covered by a Node unit test (tests/gpu-adapter.test.mjs) instead; still a real gap until a live device-loss event is captured.

codeChangesUnderTest.change: Found live, not anticipated by the plan text: the chain-broken handler's fast path (resolve every entry in `this.waiting` immediately) only helps a lap that is already in flight at the instant the mesh 'left' event fires. A lap that starts AFTER that -- sent to `this.next`, which is not repointed until _recover() actually runs -- fell through to the plain 20000 ms setTimeout inside _step(). Fixed by recording departed ids in a new `this._deadPeers` Set in the 'left' handler, and having _step() throw immediately if `this.next` is already in it.
codeChangesUnderTest.evidence: See runs 2 and 3 below: identical kill timing, only the fix differed. chain-broken -> recovering went from 20037 ms to 28 ms.

runs.note: First live attempt, unscripted timing -- the kill landed near the tail of a 60-token generation (at the trailing '<|im_end|>\n' turn-closer, after gen-done had already fired for the visible answer), not mid-loop. Predates the dead-peer fix.
runs.outcome: Recovered; answer text read as one coherent, non-restarted, non-garbled continuation.

runs.note: Instrumented repeat, predates the dead-peer fix. Prompt was sent and the worker was dropped in the same batched tool call (minimal gap) to land the kill as early as possible -- which, combined with the bug this run exposes, meant the very first post-kill lap was sent into the void.
runs.diagnosis: Matches _step()'s hardcoded 20000 ms per-lap setTimeout almost exactly -- proof the fast-fail path was not the one that fired.

runs.note: Same instrumentation and same batched send+kill timing as run 2, WITH the dead-peer fix in place. The batch landed the kill after only 1 prompt token had been fed (the earliest possible interruption point), harder than run 2's already-early timing.
runs.outcome: Recovered in 3.2 s; the post-recovery answer is token-identical to the pre-existing golden reference for the same fixed prompt, despite the disconnect landing 1 token into the conversation and the entire model being reloaded solo mid-turn.

option2_threeDeviceMiddleKill.scenario: The Option 2 case this report originally listed as not attempted: three devices, genuine 3-way split, kill the MIDDLE device mid-generation. This is the direct GPU analog of tests/recovery.test.mjs's runWithFailure(1, "the middle device leaves"), and is harder than Option 1 because the chain topology must be re-ordered rather than merely shrunk.

kill.method: room.dropWorker(room.chain[0]) -- the same code path an unplanned disconnect takes

option2_threeDeviceMiddleKill.rePlan: The surviving worker, which had held [19,28), was re-dealt [14,28); the host grew from [0,10) to [0,14) and re-loaded 380.9 MB. A genuine re-order of the chain, not just a shrink.
option2_threeDeviceMiddleKill.answerOutcome: Generation continued to a natural finish: 182 tokens at 9.25 tok/s, median hop 21.8 ms, a complete <think> block with a closing </think> and a real final answer, stopping at <|im_end|> rather than hitting the 320-token cap. No 'error' or 'recover-failed' events fired.
option2_threeDeviceMiddleKill.verdict: PASS. Phase A's Option 2 is now closed on real hardware, with the same 1 ms detect-to-recover latency the two-device case showed.

step_A2_liveDeviceLoss_nowCovered.howItHappened: Qwen3 4B Q8_0 solo (36 layers, 4076.4 MB) allocated successfully, then lost the device on the first inference pass -- genuine memory exhaustion, not a validation error.

rawDeviceLost.message: A valid external Instance reference no longer exists.

step_A2_liveDeviceLoss_nowCovered.whatTheCallerSaw: GPU device lost (unknown): A valid external Instance reference no longer exists. — this worker cannot continue; it must be re-planned around.
step_A2_liveDeviceLoss_nowCovered.verdict: checkDeviceLost() did exactly its job: the failure surfaced as a named, actionable device-loss message attributable to the right cause, instead of the raw Dawn-internal exception that would otherwise have come out of an in-flight GPU call. This is the message a room would now show, and the signal _stepSafe() would turn into a re-plan.

notCoveredThisSession: Whether a partial-range-reuse optimization exists for the host's unchanged [0,14) sub-range during a range-grow recovery -- confirmed by direct observation that it does NOT: every recovery in this report reloaded all 28 layers fresh, consistent with room.js dealing whole ranges per device (see IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md section 3.4).
